extracted.intended_audience: creative writers and authors (professional and aspiring) seeking self-care and sustainable writing practices
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical guidelines for maintaining mental and physical wellness while sustaining a writing practice, including habits, scheduling, accommodations, and ways to use writing therapeutically. Focused on helping writers stay creative, productive, healthy, and happy over the long term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize writing is work and avoid burnout
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is work no matter how much you enjoy it; intensive periods are possible but will lead to exhaustion if sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Howard's marathon month (6 AM–midnight every day) showed he could push through but ultimately became empty and burnt out. Use that awareness to plan limits and avoid repeatedly pushing to physical/mental breaking points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carve out time and create boundaries (sustainability)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you set your own hours you must consciously carve out time for other things — set aside time for family, friends, and rest; create sustainable practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: Brandon sets a daily non-work block (5:30–9:30) and trained himself to 'turn the clock off.' If your job/hobby lacks structure, intentionally create boundaries so work doesn't become all-consuming. This reduces guilt about not working and preserves long-term career sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate word count/quantity with self-worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making your self-worth directly correlated with word count or visible productivity metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carve goals down to the smallest possible metric: opening the document and sitting with it for 30 minutes, writing a paragraph, or doing a single 20-minute sprint. This prevents overwhelm and preserves self-esteem during low-productivity periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tiny, time-boxed writing sprints and smallest-action goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Break work into the smallest actionable bites (e.g., 20-minute sprints) to 'crack the seal' on writing when overwhelmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victoria writes in many 20-minute sprints (even on productive days she totals ~3 hours). Neil Gaiman's rule: when you sit down, your two options are do nothing or write — remove distractions and choose the small action. Examples: open the doc for 20 minutes, think about a scene, write a paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management and structure: schedules, spreadsheets, and set blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt explicit time-management systems and structure (spreadsheets, fixed times) to keep productivity balanced with life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brandon uses spreadsheets and fixed time blocks to manage family and work conflicts. If you need structure, schedule writing times and non-writing times; adjust as life requires to avoid encroachment and guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include physical self-care and pass-fail restorative activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate short, pass-fail self-care activities (yoga, stretching, baths, facemasks, walks) that do not carry productivity metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victoria recommends ~30 minutes a day of something restorative that can't be measured as 'productive' so you can pass without failing; examples: yoga, long shower, watching a show. The point is resetting rather than achieving measurable output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt routines and accommodations for physical ailments
rubrics_metrics.description: Be willing to change routines, tools, or ergonomics when dealing with chronic or acute physical issues (standing desks, different keyboards, alternate setups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan's approach: try different accommodations (standing desk, different keyboard layout) to continue working through periods of pain. Experiment to see what sticks; some accommodations may become long-term fixtures if they help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to healthcare professionals and prioritize health over 'get it done' behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about coping strategies that harm health (overusing medication, ignoring medical advice); heed professionals and others who can warn you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard's anecdote about ibuprofen causing long-term issues: some 'heroic' strategies to push through work can have lasting negative consequences. If a doctor or trusted person advises against something, reconsider it even if it boosts short-term output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external accountability to avoid overdoing it
rubrics_metrics.description: Make yourself accountable to someone (partner, friend) who can check in and signal when you are neglecting basic needs or burning out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan suggests simple check-ins ('You haven't eaten today') to force breaks. If you have someone who can call you out, they'll help you maintain balance; if not, find ways to create external checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing as therapy with caution: write to have written, not necessarily to be read
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing can be cathartic, but when used as therapy it may be best kept private or disposable; the goal is processing, not publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard: write offline or in a non-digital medium, print and delete, or physically tear the paper and let it 'flutter away.' Victoria: catharsis is useful but be mindful about how personal grievances are used in work that might be published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline and block emotional beats so you can write scenes when emotionally ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Use outlining so you can write emotional scenes out of order when you are in the right emotional state for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victoria outlines rigidly to prepare emotional beats and then writes them when she feels ready — some difficult scenes require particular mental states, and preparing them in the outline lets you work selectively without stalling the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow creative fallow periods and replenish the creative well
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that sometimes the best response is not to write; use fallow periods to consume media and replenish creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victoria: reading, watching shows, or consuming comics/films during low-writing periods helps refill inspiration. Writing also includes thinking, deleting, walking, and musing — these are valid contributions to your practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a lifestyle tracker to monitor craft and non-craft habits daily
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a simple grid tracking several craft-related and non-craft activities across days to visualize progress and maintain momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victoria's homework: put >=3 craft items (reading, writing, plotting) and >=3 non-craft items (healthy eating, walking, stretching) down the side, dates across top, track for 10–30 days. Color squares when done; the tracker makes each day a fresh start and prevents 'a day becomes a month' loss of time awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Switch mediums (pen & paper) to reduce digital distractions and reopen creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: If screens and distractions are blocking you, switch to pen and paper to lower barriers and encourage rough, noncommittal output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victoria: scribble at the top of the page so it's no longer blank, doodle, or plot by hand. This often produces usable thinking even if much of it is discarded; it helps reopen the creative door by lessening the 'official' feeling of a typed document.
